---
title: "Seasonal Temperature Trends and Urbanization Relationships around Buffalo, NY(2001–2025)"
author: Linwei Wu
date: 11/01/2026
date-format: long

# Introduction
  Rising temperatures are a major concern under global climate change, but
warming can also be influenced by local factors. Urbanization is one such factor, as
the expansion of impervious surfaces such as roads, buildings, and parking lots may
affect local temperatures. These surfaces can absorb and store heat, which may make 
urban areas warmer than surrounding rural areas.
  Western New York is an interesting area for studying these changes because it 
includes both urban and rural areas. The study area includes five counties in Western 
New York: Erie, Niagara, Chautauqua, Cattaraugus, and Allegany. These counties have 
different levels of development, providing an opportunity to examine the relationship 
between warming and urbanization. Temperature changes may also vary across different 
months, and minimum and maximum temperatures may not increase at the same rate.
  This project examines temperature trends in five counties in Western New York from 
2001 to 2025. It focuses on three research questions:
1. How did temperature trends change across four representative months: January, April, 
July, and October?
2. Did weather stations with greater increases in impervious surfaces show stronger 
warming trends?
3. How did minimum temperature (TMIN) trends compare with maximum temperature (TMAX) 
trends across different months, and how did these differences vary with impervious 
surface changes?

# Materials and methods
  This project uses three main datasets: temperature, impervious surface, and county 
boundary data. Daily temperature records from 2001 to 2025 were downloaded from the 
NOAA Global Historical Climatology Network-Daily (GHCN-Daily). County boundaries were 
obtained from the U.S. Census Bureau to select weather stations within the five counties 
in Western New York. Impervious surface data for 2001 and 2025 were obtained from the 
National Land Cover Database (NLCD).
  For the temperature data, I first cleaned the daily records and removed missing or 
invalid values. Daily maximum temperature (TMAX) and minimum temperature (TMIN) were used 
to calculate average temperature (TAVG). The daily data were then converted into monthly 
averages. I kept months with at least 80% valid daily observations and stations with at 
least 95% monthly completeness. January, April, July, and October were selected to represent 
winter, spring, summer, and fall. Linear regression was used to calculate temperature trends 
for each station and month from 2001 to 2025.
  For the NLCD data, I created a 2 km buffer around each weather station and calculated the 
mean impervious surface percentage for both years. The difference between 2025 and 2001 was 
used to measure urbanization change.
  Finally, I combined the temperature trends and impervious surface changes using station 
IDs to examine their relationships.

## Download and clean all required data

```{r}
n=20
data=data.frame(x=runif(n,-180,180),
                y=runif(n,-60,60),
                size = runif(n, 5, 20),
                category = factor(
                  sample(letters[1:5], n, replace = TRUE)
                  ),
                value = rnorm(n))
```

```{r, results='asis'}
data %>% 
  slice(1:10) %>% #show only 1:n rows
  kable(digits=2,align="c")%>% #make table and round to two digits
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = 
                  c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive")) #apply other formatting
```
